result.summary: This draft PR specializes single-byte serialization paths across AutoFile, DataStream, VectorWriter, SizeComputer, and CSHA256/CHash256 to avoid unnecessary allocations and memcpy calls, using std::span static extents enabled by a prior PR. It merges several serialization/deserialization template overloads with if-constexpr branches and adds new benchmarks (SerializeBlock, SizeComputerBlock) alongside the existing DeserializeBlock benchmarks. It is part of a longer-running tracking effort to speed up IBD.
result.problem: Block (de)serialization performs many single-byte writes (for uint8_t, bool, VarInt/CompactSize prefixes) that currently go through generalized buffer-allocating paths; the author profiled this as a hot spot. The benefit for real-world workloads (versus buffered readers/writers already used in the hot path) has been repeatedly questioned by reviewers.

open_concerns: maflcko has repeatedly asked what real code path benefits, noting that AutoFile writes normally go through BufferedReader/Writer and 1-byte writes there don't reach AutoFile directly; unclear how kernel or IBD is actually affected
sedited could not reproduce clear speedups locally and questioned whether the sha256 single-byte Write specialization is worth its complexity
Author himself calls the single-byte specializations 'ugly' and has not found a cleaner approach
maflcko suggested an alternative architecture (buffered writer behind a compilation boundary, per a blog post) that might achieve the same or better results without these specializations
resolved_concerns: Waiting on #31519 (std::span static extents) was resolved when that PR merged and this one was rebased on top

categories.name: tests
categories.evidence: Adds SizeComputerBlock and SerializeBlock benchmarks in src/bench/checkblock.cpp and renames existing benchmarks; touches fuzz/autofile.cpp and streams_tests.cpp only mechanically to update call sites for the new span-based API.
categories.rationale: P3 because the new benchmarks give visibility into block (de)serialization cost, which is useful framework capability, but they measure a narrow internal code path whose real-world relevance is disputed by maflcko, and the fuzz/unit test edits are purely mechanical call-site updates for the span API change.

categories.name: utils
categories.evidence: Directly modifies core serialization infrastructure (serialize.h), stream classes (streams.h/cpp), hashing helpers (hash.h), and CSHA256 (crypto/sha256.h/cpp) to add single-byte specializations and merge template overloads with if-constexpr.
categories.rationale: P3 because this is a performance change to a widely shared serialization/hashing utility, which matters on its own terms per the utils rubric, but the claimed real-world payoff (IBD speedup, kernel benefit) has been repeatedly disputed by maflcko as unclear given buffered I/O already sits between AutoFile and the hot loop, and the author himself has not landed on a clean implementation after over a year of iteration ('I don't like all the specializations').

uncertainties: Whether the measured microbenchmark speedups translate into any observable IBD or kernel-consumer benefit remains unresolved in the discussion itself, not just my assessment.
The PR has been open 579 days with 12 force-pushes and remains draft with no clear target date; unclear if the author's promised rework will materially change the approach or just polish it.
result.card: This draft PR specializes single-byte serialization/deserialization paths (AutoFile, DataStream, VectorWriter, SizeComputer, CSHA256, CHash256/CHash160) to reduce allocation and memcpy overhead, building on a prior std::span static-extent change, and adds new SerializeBlock/SizeComputerBlock benchmarks. It is framed as part of the long-running IBD speedup tracking project (#32043), but the author's own description says IBD wasn't the main motivation, and maintainer maflcko has repeatedly and specifically questioned whether the change has any real-world effect since AutoFile writes are normally routed through a BufferedReader/Writer that this PR does not touch. The author has not disputed this but instead repeatedly paused the PR to rework the single-byte specializations, which he himself calls 'ugly', with a newer rebased branch mentioned as of 2026-06-30 but not yet pushed. The PR needs rebase and is not close to a settled design, so review now risks being invalidated by the promised rework. No dependency blocks it structurally, but its value proposition remains the central open question after 17 months of discussion.
